item.title: Using the playground
item.description:
The playground runs a notebook in the browser, with no server. Go cells run in an interpreter compiled to WebAssembly; Ruby cells run in rbgo. These are its controls from go-notebook/playground v0.6.0. The keys are Jupyter’s, with the same meanings; every key has a button too, because a phone has no keyboard.

The Markdown is the notebook

A notebook is a Markdown file whose ```go and ```ruby blocks are cells. In the playground every edit goes through the same format package the notebook command uses, and the file is written back from it. Download .md gives back what you opened, byte for byte (~~~ fences and fence options included), plus your edits and nothing else. Open .md reads a local file with the same rules.

Editing a cell

Type in a cell to edit it. The cell says editing and has a solid outline. Esc selects the cell instead: it says selected and has a dashed outline, and the keys below act on the whole cell. Enter edits it again. A Markdown cell shows as text; its Edit button, or Enter, opens its source, and Esc shows it as text again.

button key on a selected cell
run this cell (and the cells above it) ▶ Run Shift+Enter, Ctrl/⌘+Enter (also while editing)
run every cell Run all
add a cell + Add cell between the cells and at the end A above, B below; Alt+Enter runs and adds below
change its language the language menu on the cell M Markdown, Y code
delete it Delete D D
undo the delete Undo delete Z
move it ↑ ↓ Ctrl+Shift+↑ / ↓

On a narrow screen a cell’s buttons fold behind ⋯.

Choosing and changing a language

+ Add cell asks what the new cell is: Go, Ruby, Julia or Markdown. A Julia cell is parsed and checked, not run yet, and the menu says so (Julia · not runnable yet); a cell that reads it is shown as blocked. The language of the code cell above comes first, marked (as above). A cell’s language menu changes the language later. Only the fence changes, from ```ruby to ```go for instance. The code is not translated, and the cell says so. Then the cell runs again.

A fenced block in any other language is not a cell. It stays text, marked not run: shown as text.

Running

The playground keeps no values between runs, and it has no dependency graph. So running a cell runs every cell above it too, in order, and none of the cells below it; those keep their last results, greyed until they run again. The notebook command does more: its kernel orders the cells by what they use and runs only what changed (the kernel).

Limits

A notebook you open may come from anyone. The playground gives it:

  • 30 s per cell. A cell that runs longer is stopped as the kernel’s --timeout stops it: stopped: the cell ran longer than 30s, the limit; its worker was killed. The next run starts a fresh runtime.
  • 1 MiB per notebook. A larger file is refused when opened.
  • No memory limit, unlike the kernel’s --memory. The page cannot bound the heap of the WebAssembly worker while a cell runs; the browser’s own limit is the only one.
  • No network, no file system and no access to the page, in Go or in Ruby. Every figure goes through two SVG sanitizers before it is shown.

Where the controls come from

The gestures follow Jupyter Notebook 7 and JupyterLab, read in their sources:

  • jupyterlab/jupyterlab:
    • docs/source/user/notebook.md: edit and command modes;
    • packages/notebook-extension/schema/tracker.json: the keys;
    • packages/notebook/src/notebookfooter.ts: the add button after the last cell;
    • packages/notebook/src/default-toolbar.tsx: the cell type menu;
    • packages/cell-toolbar-extension/schema/plugin.json: the cell toolbar.
  • The language per cell follows Polyglot Notebooks (the dotnet/interactive README), where each cell names its own language.
